1. Entering and Revising Data

A. Efficient Data Entry Mechanisms

Beyond manual typing, modern spreadsheet applications provide automation tools to accelerate data entry and prevent human error:

  1. The Fill Handle & AutoFill:

    • The Fill Handle: The small green/black square located at the bottom-right corner of the active cell or selection.
    • AutoFill: Recognizes logical sequences and extends them across adjacent cells when the handle is dragged:
      • Standard Series: Days of the week (Mon, Tue), months (Jan, Feb), dates (01/01/2026, 01/02/2026).
      • Alphanumeric Codes: Item 1, Item 2 $\rightarrow$ automatically increments to Item 3, Item 4.
      • Custom Numerical Series: Enter two seed values (e.g., 5, 10), highlight both, and drag to increment by step intervals of $5$.
      • Modifier Keys: Holding Ctrl while dragging a single numeric cell forces an incremental series instead of copying the value.

  2. Flash Fill (Ctrl + E):

    • An intelligent data-transformation feature that detects patterns in user entry and automatically completes the remaining column.
    • Common Use Cases:
      • Splitting Data: Extracting first and last names from a full-name column (Jane Doe $\rightarrow$ Jane).
      • Concatenation: Combining separate columns (e.g., merging First Name and Last Name into an email address john.smith@company.com).
      • Formatting: Adding hyphens, dashes, or parentheses to plain numbers (e.g., converting 9876543210 to (987) 654-3210).

  3. Auto-Complete for Text:

    • When typing text in a column, Excel suggests an entry if the first few letters match an existing entry in that same column. Press Enter to accept or keep typing to ignore.
    • Shortcut: Press Alt + Down Arrow to display a drop-down pick-list of unique items already entered in that column.

B. Revising Existing Data

  • In-Cell Editing: Press F2 or double-click to place the insertion point inside the cell.
  • Overwriting: Single-click the cell and begin typing; all prior contents are replaced instantly.
  • Undo & Redo:
    • Ctrl + Z: Reverts the last action (can undo multiple sequential steps).
    • Ctrl + Y: Re-applies an action that was undone, or repeats the last command.

2. Moving Data Within a Workbook

Data can be reorganized within a single worksheet, between different worksheets, or across distinct workbooks.

A. Drag-and-Drop Method

Best suited for small distances within the visible screen:

  1. Select the cell or range of cells.
  2. Hover the mouse cursor over the outer border of the selection until the pointer transforms into a four-headed arrow (Windows) or a hand icon (macOS).
  3. Click and drag the border to the target location.
  4. Variations:
    • Copy instead of Move: Hold down the Ctrl key while dragging (a small + appears next to the cursor).
    • Insert between cells: Hold down the Shift key while dragging. A thin horizontal or vertical insertion bar will indicate where existing cells will shift to make room without overwriting.

B. Cut, Copy, and Paste Operations

  • Cut (Ctrl + X): Marks the selected data with a "marching ants" marquee border. Removes the data from its original location once pasted.
  • Copy (Ctrl + C): Duplicates the data onto the clipboard while leaving original cells intact.
  • Paste (Ctrl + V): Places cut or copied items into the designated target cell.

C. Moving Data Across Sheets and Workbooks

  1. Cut / Copy the source data (Ctrl + X or Ctrl + C).
  2. Switch to the target sheet using the bottom tabs (or shortcut Ctrl + Page Down / Ctrl + Page Up).
  3. Click the destination anchor cell (top-left of target range) and press Ctrl + V.
  4. Inserting Cut Cells: To avoid overwriting existing data at the destination, right-click the destination cell and choose Insert Cut Cells (or Insert Copied Cells), then specify whether existing cells should shift Down or Right.

D. The Office Clipboard

  • Accessible via Home tab $\rightarrow$ click the small dialog box launcher arrow in the Clipboard group.
  • Collects up to 24 items across Microsoft Office apps.
  • Allows you to copy multiple non-contiguous elements from various locations and paste them individually or all at once using Paste All.

3. Finding and Replacing Data

The Find & Replace tool is essential for managing, auditing, and bulk-correcting large datasets.

Accessing the Tools:
• Find Dialog:    Ctrl + F
• Replace Dialog: Ctrl + H

A. Basic and Advanced Search Parameters

Clicking Options >> inside the Find/Replace window reveals advanced search controls:

Search Parameter Function
Within Toggles search boundary between the current Sheet or the entire Workbook.
Search Determines scan direction: By Rows (scans across) or By Columns (scans down).
Look in Restricts search to:
• Formulas (scans underlying syntax).
• Values (scans final evaluated results).
• Notes / Comments (scans annotations).
Match case Enforces case-sensitivity (e.g., searching Smith will skip smith or SMITH).
Match entire cell contents Cell must contain only the search string. Searching Cat will not return Catalog or Scatter.

B. Using Wildcard Characters

Wildcards allow for flexible search patterns when exact spellings or complete words are unknown:

  • Asterisk (*): Represents any number of consecutive characters (zero or more).
    • Example: East* finds East, Eastern, Eastside, East-Coast.
  • Question Mark (?): Represents exactly one single character.
    • Example: H?ll finds Hall, Hell, Hill, Hull (but not Hotel).
  • Tilde (~): Used as an escape character to find literal wildcards.
    • Example: To find an actual question mark in a cell, search for ~?; to find an actual asterisk, search for ~*.

4. Correcting and Expanding Upon Worksheet Data

A. Proofing Tools: Spell Check & AutoCorrect

  • Spelling Check (F7): Scans the active sheet for spelling errors against the standard dictionary.
    • Limitation: Does not check text embedded inside mathematical formulas or numbers.
  • AutoCorrect Options:
    • Located via File $\rightarrow$ Options $\rightarrow$ Proofing $\rightarrow$ AutoCorrect Options...
    • Automatically fixes common typing mistakes (e.g., changing teh to the).
    • Can be customized to create shorthand text expansions (e.g., typing dept can automatically expand to Department of Transportation).

B. Modifying Structure: Rows, Columns, and Cells

  1. Inserting Rows & Columns:
    • Rows are always inserted above the selected row.
    • Columns are always inserted to the left of the selected column.
    • Shortcuts:
      • Select a row/column, then press Ctrl + Shift + + (Plus key).
      • To select an entire row: Shift + Spacebar.
      • To select an entire column: Ctrl + Spacebar.
  2. Deleting Rows & Columns:
    • Select row/column and press Ctrl + - (Minus key).
  3. AutoFit Dimensions:
    • Double-click the separator line between two column headers (e.g., between B and C) to automatically expand column width to fit the longest entry.
    • Double-click between row headers to AutoFit row height.

C. Expanding with "Paste Special"

Accessed by copying data (Ctrl + C), right-clicking destination $\rightarrow$ Paste Special... (Shortcut: Ctrl + Alt + V):

  • Paste Values: Strips all underlying formulas, macros, and source formatting, pasting only static, calculated results (useful when finalizing reports).
  • Paste Formats: Applies only styles, colors, and borders without altering cell contents.
  • Paste Column Widths: Copies the exact column widths of source data to target columns.
  • Transpose: Rotates data orientation—swaps rows to columns, or columns to rows:

$$\begin{matrix} \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} \end{matrix} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Transpose}} \quad \begin{matrix} \text{A} \ \text{B} \ \text{C} \end{matrix}$$

  • Mathematical Operations: Enables bulk arithmetic without formulas. For instance, copying a cell containing the value 1.10, selecting a price column, and choosing Paste Special $\rightarrow$ Multiply instantly increases all prices by $10%$.

5. Defining and Working with Tables

In modern spreadsheet programs, an official Table (also known as an Excel Table or ListObject) is fundamentally different from a simple range of formatted grid cells.

A. Range vs. Table: Key Differences

Feature Standard Cell Range Formal Table
Identification Addressed by cell coordinates (A1:E20) Addressed by a unique name (e.g., SalesTable)
Formatting Applied manually cell-by-cell Automatic alternate-color row banding and styles
Expansion Adding data requires re-formatting/re-ranging Dynamic expansion: New rows/columns auto-integrate
Formulas Requires manual drag-down to copy formulas Calculated Columns: Formulas auto-fill down entire column
Header Row Scrolls off the screen unless Freeze Panes is set Header row automatically replaces column letters when scrolling

B. Creating a Table

  1. Click anywhere inside the dataset (ensure headers exist and there are no completely blank rows/columns dividing the data).
  2. Go to Insert $\rightarrow$ Table or press the keyboard shortcut:
    • Ctrl + T or Ctrl + L
  3. Verify the detected data range in the dialog box.
  4. Ensure the checkbox "My table has headers" is checked $\rightarrow$ click OK.

C. Anatomy and Core Features of a Table

When a cell inside a table is active, the contextual Table Design tab appears on the Ribbon.

  1. Table Name:
    • Found at the far-left of the Table Design tab.
    • Rename generic names (e.g., Table1) to descriptive identifiers (e.g., StaffDirectory, Sales2026). Spaces are not allowed; use camelCase or underscores.
  2. Auto-Filter Buttons:
    • Drop-down filter arrows are automatically placed on every header cell, enabling instant Sorting (A-Z, Z-A) and Filtering by criteria/colors.
  3. Banded Rows & Columns:
    • Checkboxes that instantly apply alternating background shading to improve readability across wide sets of data.
  4. Calculated Columns:
    • Typing a formula in any cell of a table column and hitting Enter automatically propagates that exact calculation to every single row in that column.
  5. The Total Row (Ctrl + Shift + T):
    • Toggling this on appends a summary row to the bottom of the table.
    • Clicking on any cell in the Total Row presents a drop-down menu containing aggregate functions (SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX, MIN, STDDEV).
    • Formulas use the =SUBTOTAL() function under the hood, meaning hidden/filtered rows are automatically excluded from the displayed total.

D. Structured References

Tables replace cryptic coordinate addresses with intuitive, syntax-based references using column names:

  • Standard Range formula: =C2 * D2
  • Table Structured Reference: =[@UnitPrice] * [@Quantity]
    • The @ symbol denotes “this current row”.
    • Referencing an entire column from outside the table: =SUM(SalesTable[TotalAmount]).
    • Benefits: Formulas are self-documenting, less prone to offset errors, and auto-update if the table changes size.

E. Resizing and Converting Tables

  • Automatic Growth: Typing data directly in the blank row immediately below the table, or the blank column immediately to the right, automatically incorporates that new data into the table boundary.
  • Manual Resize: Click and drag the small sizing angle handle at the bottom-right corner of the table.
  • Converting Back to a Normal Range:
    • If table behavior is no longer desired: Go to Table Design tab $\rightarrow$ click Convert to Range (or right-click table $\rightarrow$ Table $\rightarrow$ Convert to Range).
    • Cell data and visual styles are preserved, but dynamic functionality (structured formulas, automatic filters, table names) is removed.
